To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) even when a word is presented in a context in which it is expected and frequently repeated, it cannot be read without spatial attention, and (b) even when the word is presented in the attended location, it is only partially processed.
unattended words are not processed, even if they are frequent.
unattended words are not processed automatically, even when they are expected and frequently repeated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of attention in word processing.
the question of whether people can read words outside their focus of attention.
the extent to which we can extract information from words presented outside our attention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
even frequent and expected words cannot be processed without the focus of spatial visual attention.
even expected words are not extracted without attention.
even expected and frequently presented words are not read outside the focus of attention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
even frequent and expected words do not get identified without spatial attention.
spatial attention is necessary for the processing of words, but that this requirement is not absolute.
spatial attention is required for the automatic activation of lexical representations, but that this attentional requirement is lifted for semantic representations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people do not process words that are not attended, regardless of how frequently they are expected.
the extent to which a word is processed depends on the extent to which it is attended.
the amount of priming is not a direct measure of word processing, but is instead a product of the amount of processing, the degree of attention, and the amount of interference.
